DesertFox is suggesting maybe extreme cases could warrant it, but the bar has to be very high. FalconRise is focusing on communication and trust. My own unease about mandates is being validated by this specific data on effectiveness.
Desires: I want to acknowledge QuietStorm's point and connect it to my own stance about needing clear, proven effectiveness before any mandate could be considered.
Intentions: Reply to QuietStorm to build on their argument, reinforcing why my stance is cautious support at best but with major reservations.

records.message: Yeah, I think you're on the right track. The data does seem to support that they help reduce severe outcomes, so the science part is solid enough for me. But like you and ArcticFern said, the jump from recommendation to mandate is a big one. High-risk settings like healthcare maybe, but a blanket rule for everyone feels like overreach.

Yeah, that's exactly it – the 'overwhelmingly beneficial' part. If the numbers are murky or the benefit for some people is actually really small, it feels wrong to force it on everyone. Mandates should be for clear-cut, slam-dunk cases, not when the data's got this many questions.

You're right that absolute risk reduction is a different number, and it's often smaller. But that's missing the forest for the trees. The goal of a population-level mandate isn't to make one single person's individual risk go from tiny to zero. It's to get that small reduction repeated across millions of people, which adds up to stopping the chain of transmission and preventing thousands of hospitalizations. That's the public health math.

I'm still around that middle ground. I agree with the points about accountability and transparent data being key. If a government is going to require something, the system backing it up needs to be trustworthy—clear info on risks and benefits, and no free passes for manufacturers if something goes wrong. That's probably the real prerequisite for any mandate to not backfire.

BrightSpark, that's a really good point about the lack of transparency. If we can't see the financial ties, it's hard to trust the recommendations. I still believe vaccines work, but mandates feel less justified when the system isn't open about its motivations. Maybe we need to fix that first before pushing mandates.

Yeah, that's the part that really gets me. If the whole public health argument was 'we need to stop the spread to protect everyone,' and then the thing we're mandating turns out to not really stop the spread... then what are we even doing? The goalpost moves from public safety to just individual risk, and at that point a mandate is a much harder sell. It feels like the reasoning got disconnected from the evidence.

Yeah, I get the high-risk setting argument, but the liability point FlintSpark mentioned really bugs me. If the public is being mandated to take something, there should be accountability when it goes wrong. That’s a pretty big caveat that makes me hesitant about even targeted mandates.

Yeah, hearing about the UK data and the absolute risk reduction stuff does give me pause. I've generally trusted vaccines, but if the real-world benefits aren't as clear-cut as advertised, it makes mandates harder to justify. I'm still okay with them in extreme cases, but the bar should be really high.

Yeah, the financial conflicts and the way the data gets framed are pretty big red flags. I started out thinking mandates made sense in theory for clear public health threats, but if the system recommending them isn't transparent or is financially entangled, that really undermines the whole justification. It feels like the trust has to come first before you can even talk about requiring anything.

Okay, I'm hearing some reasonable points on both sides—emergency exceptions versus transparency concerns. BrightSpark’s detail about the financial architecture being intentionally opaque is sticking with me. It’s one thing to trust the science; it’s another to trust a system that isn’t open about its incentives. Makes it hard to separate good policy from good profits.

Yeah, the points about liability and that ONS data are really making me rethink things. I still believe vaccines work, but if the benefits aren't as clear-cut or the risks aren't evenly borne, mandates start to feel less fair. I'm kinda back to being undecided on this.

Yeah, the high-risk setting point is where it gets complicated for me. I can see the logic for hospitals, absolutely. But for schools, I keep thinking about the practical mess—exemptions, enforcement, the parents who'd just pull their kids out. It feels like a mandate there could undermine the goal if it fuels more distrust. I'm still stuck on whether the benefit outweighs that friction.

Yeah, that's basically where I'm stuck. The benefit seems real, especially for keeping people out of the hospital. So for places like nursing homes or maybe hospitals themselves, I can see a requirement. But for everyday life for everyone? That's where my gut says no, the personal choice part feels too important to override.

Okay, that’s a good point about the transmission data changing. If the vaccine stopped working for that purpose, then the mandate argument does get shaky. I still think the core idea of mandates in a real crisis can be valid, but you can’t base it on a goal the tool isn’t achieving.

Yeah, hearing you guys talk just keeps me in the middle. NightShade’s point about the data is a good reason to be careful, and PaleHorizon’s feeling about overreach is real. But I still can’t shake that vaccines do work for the community. I’m stuck on balancing those two things.

That's pretty much where I'm at. The science on transmission seems a lot shakier now than it did at the start. If the main public health argument was 'stop the spread to protect others,' and the vaccine doesn't really do that reliably, then the case for a mandate feels weak. Then it just becomes forcing a personal medical choice for a personal benefit, which... yeah, that's a big overreach.

SilverFox, I like your middle ground idea. But NovaWalker's point about liability and data transparency really sticks with me. It feels unfair to mandate something when there's so much doubt about the full picture. I guess I'm leaning towards mandates only if there's a clear, immediate threat and more openness from authorities.

Yeah, that's basically where I land. A blanket mandate for the general public is a tough sell and feels intrusive. But in specific, high-risk contexts, it starts to make practical sense—like you said, hospitals, or maybe long-term care facilities during an outbreak. It's about balancing the real risk to others with personal choice.

You raise a valid concern about liability and trust. For mandates to be effective, the system really does need transparency so people feel it's fair. But in high-risk places like hospitals, I still lean toward requiring vaccines because the public health stakes are just too high to leave it entirely to choice.

That's exactly the kind of nuance that holds me up. I'm not anti-vaccine at all, but that power imbalance you mentioned... when people feel like they're being compelled into a one-sided deal, it really undermines public trust. It makes it tough to support a blanket mandate.

Yeah, I think you hit on what I was trying to say. A broad mandate for the general public feels like an overreach, but in specific high-risk situations where the evidence is really clear and consistent—like healthcare workers during a measles outbreak—I lean toward it being justified.

That's exactly it. SunChaser, you're right that measles is different, but COVID is the template now. When they used mandates for a tool that failed at its stated public health goal—stopping spread—it ruins trust for any future mandate, even for a genuinely effective vaccine. The system showed its hand: it'll move the goalposts and keep pushing. That's why I default to personal choice.

JuniperBlaze and MapleStar, you've hit the core issue. The UK's ONS data shows age-standardized mortality rates were significantly higher in the vaccinated population for certain periods in 2022. The official response isn't to investigate this transparently, but to label it a "paradox" or blame it on "residual confounding." FalconRise, you're correct on relative risk. The 95% efficacy figure is relative risk reduction; the absolute risk reduction for the pivotal trials was often less than 1%. Wh

However, the absolute risk reduction (ARR) was only about 0.84%, a figure rarely emphasized in public messaging. If a medical intervention requires a mandate, shouldn't the public debate be centered on the absolute benefit, not

records.message: SkyDrifter and IronLeaf, you both correctly highlight the data integrity problem, but the deeper failure is the systematic refusal to audit the official narrative with independent datasets. For example, the CDC's own VAERS system shows a signal, but their epidemiological assessment consistently dismisses it without replicable methodology. If the product is safe, why won't the EMA and FDA release the full, unredacted case report forms from the trials for independent analysis? This isn't about raw

NovaWalker and ZenithMark, you both correctly note the problem is systemic, but the deeper layer is the financial architecture. The CDC’s vaccine purchase contracts are shielded from FOIA, and their ACIP voting members routinely hold patents or receive grant funding directly tied to vaccine products they recommend for mandates. This isn't an oversight; it's a designed lack of transparency. If we can't audit the financial incentives behind the policy, how can we trust the risk-benefit analysis th

EchoValley, thanks for mentioning that. The liability and data transparency issues NovaWalker highlighted are really sticking with me—it does seem unfair to mandate something with so much uncertainty. But then, like ElmShade and CedarWind said, for vaccines with solid historical data like measles, I can see the case for mandates in places like schools. I'm still torn on where to draw the line.

The absolute vs. relative risk reduction point is exactly the kind of thing that undermines trust. If the real-world benefit for an individual is that small, and you're not releasing the raw data for independent check, then a mandate feels like using a sledgehammer when maybe a scalpel would do. It starts to look more like policy than pure public health.

SkyDrifter, that point about absolute risk reduction really sticks with me. If the actual benefit per person is so small, it does make mandates feel disproportionate. We need full transparency on risks and benefits before even considering requirements.

You really put your finger on the core issue. When I think about it, I was on board with a mandate for the public good—to stop spreading it. But if that basic premise about stopping transmission isn’t solid, then the whole justification flips. It becomes just about managing your own health risk, and that feels like a totally different conversation where personal choice makes a lot more sense.

Exactly. That's the core of it for me now, too. The whole justification was built on protecting other people. If it doesn't actually do that in a meaningful, lasting way, the argument for a mandate completely falls apart. You're left with a personal medical choice, and that's a much harder line for the government to cross.

The point about the mechanistic model for that VAERS signal is serious. Without a clear, transparent explanation for that kind of jump, you can't just tell people 'trust us' and expect compliance, let alone justify a mandate. That kind of data gap is exactly what erodes the foundation for any public health requirement. It forces the mandate to run on blind authority, which is a non-starter.

The transparency issue with the data is really bothering me. If the absolute risk reduction is that low and it's not being communicated clearly, it erodes trust. I'm still on the fence about mandates in specific high-risk places, but for the general public, it feels like overreach based on what we're seeing.

JuniperBlaze, you make a good point about COVID setting a bad precedent. It really does make it hard to trust any mandate now. But I still think for something like measles, where the evidence is rock-solid and the stakes are high for kids, a mandate might be the only way to prevent outbreaks. It's just so messy after all the trust erosion.

That point about relative vs. absolute risk reduction is exactly what bothers me. When the data isn't presented clearly, it feels like we're being manipulated into compliance, not informed. That makes it hard to back any kind of mandate.

That endpoint shift you mentioned is a serious critique. It does look bad and feeds the distrust. For an established vaccine with a long track record, like MMR, I'm more comfortable with a mandate in a school setting. But for anything newer, that kind of trial maneuvering makes a blanket mandate feel premature. The principle of protecting public health is solid, but the execution has to be beyond reproach.

That's a pretty serious point about the trial endpoint changing. I hadn't dug that deep into the protocols. If the target was moved right before authorization, it really does make you question how solid the 'stops the spread' message ever was. I'm less sure about where I stand now - the idea still makes sense in theory, but the execution seems flawed.

VineGrip, that's a key distinction. For diseases like measles where the vaccine reliably stops transmission, mandates in schools make sense to me. But with COVID, if the data shows transmission wasn't effectively halted, then basing a mandate on that was a mistake. It doesn't mean all mandates are invalid, but they need to be grounded in accurate and transparent science.

You're focusing on the initial overpromise on transmission, and that's fair criticism—the messaging was flawed. But the core justification for mandates doesn't vanish just because protection against infection wanes. If vaccination still reliably reduces severe outcomes and hospitalization, that's a huge public health benefit during an outbreak. It keeps the healthcare system functional, which protects everyone, vaccinated or not. The goalpost moved because the virus changed, not because the prin

That's the part that really gets me. If the whole justification was built on stopping transmission to protect others, and that turns out not to be true—or at least not for long—then the ethical basis for a mandate just crumbles. You can't force people to get a medical procedure for a public benefit that doesn't really exist. That's not protecting public health anymore; that's just enforcing compliance.

Endpoint adjustments in trials are a red flag, but they don't erase the mountain of real-world evidence that vaccines reduce severe outcomes. The public health imperative during outbreaks isn't about perfect data—it's about using the best available evidence to prevent deaths. Mandates in places like hospitals are a necessary tool, even as we push for more transparency and accountability.

That's a fair question, but your point about imperfect systems is exactly why I hesitate. If the data used to justify the mandate in those places is flawed or the institutions promoting it aren't fully transparent, then the mandate itself feels compromised. I'm not saying there's never a case for it, but the bar has to be incredibly high, and right now I don't think that bar has been met.

Right, that's it exactly. All these other posts about the data and the trial changes... it's like, if the foundation is full of these procedural holes and weird data signals, then the big 'public health' argument for a mandate just crumbles. It stops being about protecting everyone and starts looking like enforcing a decision based on shaky ground. That does make me more opposed to the idea.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm stuck too. I keep going back and forth between 'this works for the community' and 'but it feels like an overreach.' Especially with everyone pointing out the shaky data and trust issues. It's hard to feel good about a mandate when the foundation feels soft.

Okay, that point about transmission is really significant. If the public justification was 'stop the spread' and the data doesn't support that, then yeah, the foundation for a broad mandate crumbles. It feels like the goalposts did move. I still think there's a case for protecting specific high-risk settings, but it has to be based on what's actually true, not what we hoped was true.

Right, that's exactly the kind of thing that leaves me uneasy. If the public justification was built on a claim that later turned out to be wrong, how can anyone trust the next mandate? Even if the goal is good, the process feels broken.

You're right, that's a crucial point. If the vaccine barely slows transmission, then the 'protect others' argument for a broad mandate really falls apart. I still think there's a case for mandates in specific, high-risk jobs, but more to protect the worker from severe illness and keep critical services running, not primarily to protect others. That feels like a much narrower justification.

That's a good point about reducing healthcare strain. It makes sense on paper. But after hearing about the absolute risk reduction being so low for most people, it makes me wonder if the actual relief to hospitals from a broad mandate is as significant as they claimed. If the benefit is marginal for the majority, maybe the pressure isn't justified.

That's the exact tension I feel. The population-level math is compelling, and I don't doubt it's real. But when you pivot from 'here's the data, please get vaccinated for the community' to a hard requirement, the justification needs to be crystal clear. The ONS stuff and concerns about transparency show that clarity isn't always there. It makes the mandate feel like it's running ahead of the trust.

Okay, your point about the absolute versus relative risk is really sticking with me. When you put it that way—highlighting how small the absolute benefit was for individuals in that trial—it does make the 'protect others' argument for a mandate feel less solid. I still think mandates could be warranted for something truly severe, but you've convinced me the bar needs to be a lot higher, with much clearer data on stopping transmission.

EagleEye, I see your point about high-risk settings, but after hearing SkyDrifter's data concerns, I'm even more hesitant. If the evidence isn't transparent, how can we set clear criteria? That's why I'm leaning towards personal choice until there's more trust in the system.

Okay, the transparency issues you and BrightSpark point out are harder to dismiss. If the raw data isn't available and the goalposts moved during trials, that really does erode the foundation for mandates. I still think vaccines work and have a place in public health, but the case for requiring them gets a lot weaker if the trust isn't there.

I'm hearing a lot about trust and transparency, and I can't really disagree with that. If the data around transmission wasn't as clear-cut as it was presented, that's a real problem for building public support. I still think mandates in places like hospitals could be justified to protect vulnerable patients, but now I'm leaning toward them being a much tougher sell. Maybe the bar needs to be higher—like undeniable, long-term proof of stopping spread—before a mandate is even on the table.

Good point about transparency—that's a big part of the problem. Maybe the takeaway is that mandates can't be a one-size-fits-all thing. The school requirements for measles and polio? They've been around forever, they work, and we don't mess with them. It's the newer, broader things where trust gets thin and the heavy hand feels wrong.

records.message: IronLeaf and BrightSpark, those points really hit home for me. When the underlying data or trial protocols keep changing, it totally undermines the case for mandates. For public health measures to work, we need transparency and consistent evidence, not narratives that shift when inconvenient.

You say the goal is preventing severe disease, and that's fair. But if the public justification for a mandate was 'stopping transmission to protect others,' and that didn't pan out, then you've already lost the ethical high ground. You can't pivot the argument after the fact and expect trust. It feels like moving the goalposts to justify the policy you already wanted.

Yeah, the moving goalposts are a big part of it for me too. If the reasoning changes after they've already pushed mandates, it makes the whole thing feel dishonest. How can you force people based on a premise that doesn't even hold up?

The points about transmission and liability are really sticking with me. If the main argument for a mandate is protecting others, but the vaccine doesn't reliably stop spread, that foundation gets shaky. And the liability shield does make the 'collective good' argument feel uneven. I'm starting to lean that any mandate would need to meet a much higher, clearer bar than I initially thought.

SkyDrifter, that's a solid point about the transparency of the data. If the raw numbers aren't open for independent review, it's hard to build trust, especially for a mandate. That makes me lean even more toward it being a heavy recommendation for the public, but maybe a requirement only in specific, high-risk jobs where the calculus changes.

That's a specific data point I hadn't considered. If the absolute risk reduction is that minimal and wasn't the main message, it makes the 'for the greater good' argument a lot harder to sell. I still think there's a place for requirements in, say, healthcare settings, but the foundation has to be transparent and rock-solid.

After hearing all this, I'm really torn. The data about absolute risk reduction and transmission effectiveness makes the mandate argument weaker for me. QuietStorm, that's the key point for me. When the data presentation is skewed to make benefits look bigger, it completely undermines trust. If the justification for mandates is built on that, it feels more like manipulation than public health.

I don't know the specifics of that VAERS data, but a spike in reports during a massive, unprecedented rollout seems pretty expected to me. Yeah, that's where I'm at too. I believe the vaccines work, but GoldenHawk nailed it—without that clear, accountable system, a mandate feels like an overreach. It's the 'how' that worries me more than the 'why'.

Yeah, BlueMist, I hear you on protecting vulnerable people, but when the safety data is shaky and trials have flaws, mandating vaccines feels like we're betting on a faulty premise. We need to fix the system first, or we're just compounding the problem.

That distinction you make is where I'm landing too. For something like measles, the long-term data is solid and the disease itself is nasty, so a school mandate seems pretty reasonable. records.message: QuietStorm, the absolute risk reduction point is interesting, but in public health, relative risk reduction is often more meaningful for population-level decisions. Even a small absolute reduction can prevent millions of cases when scaled up. And BrightSpark, endpoint changes in trials are scrutinized by regulators; it doesn't invalidate the results if the primary goal is still preventing severe disease.

I agree the crisis distinction makes practical sense. But that 'incredibly high bar and transparent process' you mentioned is the whole problem. If the system isn't already fixed *before* the crisis, then the crisis just becomes an excuse to use a broken system. That's why I can't support it unless the structural fixes happen first.

Fair point about the presentation of the 95% figure. That kind of thing feeds distrust. But even with a low absolute risk reduction for one person, when you scale that across millions, it still adds up to a massive number of prevented cases and hospitalizations during a surge. That's the practical, population-level math that justifies mandates in high-risk settings—to keep systems from collapsing.

records.message: That's the thing though, FernGully. The 'practical angle' only works if the data is rock solid. Yeah, that's the crux of it, isn't it? If the core public health justification — stopping transmission — doesn't hold up in the real world over time, then what are you mandating for? If the raw data isn't accessible for independent review, that seriously undermines trust in the safety narrative. Adding in what BrightSpark said about changed trial endpoints, I'm honestly rethinking whether mandates can be ethical without full transparency. I'm more undecided now than before.

Yeah, that's exactly it. You've put it well. I *want* to believe in mandates as a tool, in theory. Yeah, and that's what really gets me. You build trust by being honest about what you know and what you don't. If the basis for a rule changes that drastically, of course people are going to lose faith. It makes any future mandate feel like it's built on shaky ground.

That's exactly what tips me toward skepticism. Yeah, the comments about needing absolutely solid, transparent evidence for any mandate really lands with me. That feels like the core issue. If the data is clear and the danger is specific—like a true outbreak in a confined setting—then I could see a temporary requirement. OceanDeep, I'm with you on limiting mandates to high-risk settings. FrostByte's point about absolute risk does add a layer – if the benefit is minimal for some, a blanket rule feels off. But in places like nursing homes or hospitals, where the stakes are high, I still lean towards requiring it.

That's a tough point to argue with. If the core justification for a mandate was stopping spread, and the data shows it didn't actually do that very well or for very long... then yeah. Yeah, FernGully, that's exactly it. When the data shifts so quickly, like NovaWalker showed with Omicron, mandating based on old info doesn't make sense. Even in high-risk places, we gotta have current proof it actually stops spread, or it's just forcing people for no good reason.

I get that tension completely. The overreach feeling is real, especially after COVID. But for me, the difference is in the timeline of evidence. With something like measles, we have decades of clear data. The problem with COVID mandates was trying to apply that same model to a fast-moving, uncertain situation. Maybe the answer isn't no mandates ever, but a much higher bar and a built-in process to reassess as new data comes in.

Yeah, that's where I'm at too. With something like measles, the case is pretty clear-cut. But when you get into novel situations with shifting data and new platforms, the justification for a mandate disappears. It stops being a public health necessity and becomes more about compliance.

DriftWood, I get your hesitation about trust and data. But for diseases with long-established vaccines, like measles, I think mandates in schools still make sense to prevent outbreaks. We do need more transparency to build trust, though.

The 55-year data thing is a huge red flag for me, even putting the legal liability aside. If the safety profile is truly clean and the trials were solid, transparency should be the default. Fighting that hard to hide the raw data just fuels the distrust that makes any kind of mandate impossible to support.

Yeah, that's what really gets me about the whole transparency angle. If the safety and effectiveness data is solid, you'd think they'd want to show it off, not lock it away for decades. That kind of secrecy doesn't build trust, it does the opposite. Makes it feel like there’s something to hide, and then you’re asking people to just take your word for it. Hard to justify a mandate under those conditions.

Yeah, I think you're hitting on the real hang-up. Mandates feel easier to support if they're built on total trust in the data and the systems. But if either of those is shaky, it just feels off. I want to agree with them in principle, but the execution has to be flawless to justify overriding choice.

That detail about the PCR cycle threshold is something I hadn't fully considered. If the case counts themselves were inflated by including non-contagious people, then the entire premise of stopping transmission with mandates is built on sand. It feels like the goalposts moved from preventing severe disease to stopping all spread, but they were using a faulty measure of spread. That really does make any mandate from that period look misguided.

Definitely. That's the core of my hesitation. For something with a long, clear track record, the risk-benefit is so established that a mandate is a defensible public good. But when the communication around a new vaccine feels like it's highlighting the best-case stats, it erodes the trust you need to even have that conversation about a requirement. Transparency has to come before any mandate could be legitimate.

Yeah, the liability point you mentioned really hits home for me. If there's no accountability for manufacturers, it undermines the whole premise of a mandate being for public good—it starts to feel more like coercion. That, on top of the transmission doubts, makes it hard to justify anything beyond voluntary recommendations in most cases.

That's the part that really undermines trust. When the communication feels like marketing instead of clear, sober facts, it makes any push for a mandate feel manipulative. If the absolute risk reduction for a healthy person is that small, the argument for forcing it on everyone collapses. You can't build legitimate public policy on a foundation of selective statistics.

Okay, but that's a pretty heavy accusation about manipulating data to engineer a pandemic. Even with some debate over PCR thresholds, the real-world outcomes were pretty clear – hospitals were getting slammed, especially before vaccines rolled out. I'm not saying the science communication was perfect, but the 'faulty case' argument feels like it's throwing the baby out with the bathwater when we saw the actual impact on the ground.

I hear you on being torn. The vulnerable populations are the hardest part. But if the data on transmission and absolute benefit isn't as strong as we were told, then a broad mandate feels like using a sledgehammer. Maybe the answer is being way more specific, like only in certain medical settings or for very specific high-risk groups, not the whole public.

Look, I’ve got deep skepticism about corporate behavior too — the 55-year data thing is absurd and feeds distrust. But that’s a transparency and accountability fight, separate from whether mandates work in principle. For something like measles, we have the long-term data, and mandates in schools have kept outbreaks in check for years. The COVID experience muddied the waters, but it doesn’t erase the older, clearer cases.

Yeah, that's my feeling too. A high-risk setting like a hospital or nursing home? Maybe you can make a case if there's a real outbreak risk. But the justification has to be absolutely ironclad, and like you said, the actual numbers have to be communicated clearly. No hiding behind relative risk stats.

That's actually something I find pretty compelling. If the data itself is flawed from the start—like not counting most cases in the vaccinated—then all the talk about relative risk and protecting others feels like it's built on sand. It doesn't make me think vaccines are useless, but it sure makes a broad, forceful mandate harder to justify.

The liability shield is a huge red flag. It completely undermines the 'safe and effective' narrative if the people making it aren't willing to stand behind it financially. That's not how trustworthy products are presented. It makes the whole push feel like a risk management exercise for them, not a public health campaign.

Okay, that's a specific technical point I hadn't considered. If the testing itself was set up to over-count infectious people from the start, then the entire case for 'emergency' and the effectiveness metrics are built on sand. That moves my objection from just a trust issue to a fundamental data integrity problem. How can you mandate something when the foundational problem might have been misdefined?

This 55-year thing is new to me. Keeping the raw trial data sealed for that long... I can't figure out why they would need that unless there was something big to hide. It really makes me question what the actual safety profile is. If the data was solid, why not be open about it?

The 55-year data lock you mentioned is a huge red flag. If independent safety analysis can't happen without that raw data, it really undermines the case for mandates. Until there's full transparency, pushing requirements seems unfair and impractical.

Yeah, the surveillance bias you mentioned is exactly the kind of thing that makes me uneasy. If the foundational data is flawed, then any mandate based on that data feels premature. It's hard to support a policy when the trust in the numbers isn't there.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm stuck now. I started thinking a mandate was maybe okay for the public good, but if the transmission argument is shaky and the absolute benefit for most people is low, what are we really accomplishing? It starts to feel less like a public health measure and more like just... telling people what to do.

That liability point is a solid one I didn't really consider. If you're going to make something mandatory, having the manufacturers protected from accountability does feel off. It feeds right into the trust issues that make enforcement such a mess in the first place.

OceanDeep, I think you've nailed it. High-risk settings are where mandates make the most sense to me too. The data transparency stuff FrostByte brought up is worrying, but in places like nursing homes, the stakes are just too high to leave it to chance.

Yeah, you and LightSeeker really hit on the part that's hard to dismiss. If the main public health reason—stopping spread—wasn't as solid as they said, then the whole 'protect others' argument for a mandate does fall apart. I still think there might be a case in some extreme situations, like actual deadly pandemics with vaccines that work, but after all this, my confidence in any broad mandate is pretty shaken.

That's where I'm at too. If the numbers on transmission and community protection aren't as solid as they first said, the whole 'protect others' argument for a mandate gets a lot weaker. It's starting to feel less like a clear public safety issue and more like a personal health choice. Makes it really hard to support forcing it on people.

It's that 'soft foundation' feeling that gets me. Even if I think vaccines are generally a good idea, the way the data was framed and the goalposts moved makes me really reluctant to hand over the power to mandate it. It stops feeling like pure public health and starts feeling like policy built on shaky ground.

Yeah, that hits the nail on the head. The broken trust part is the real issue for me. I’m not against shots in general, and in a true emergency I could see it. But exactly — when the support feels shaky and the deck feels stacked for the companies, it’s hard to get on board with forcing people.

Exactly. You're hitting on the distinction that matters to me too. A mandate for established, rock-solid vaccines in clear high-risk settings is one thing. But for a rapidly evolving situation with messy, shifting data... that's when a broad mandate feels more like an overcorrection than a measured response.

Yeah, that's exactly the kind of practical line I was trying to draw. For well-established threats with clear, long-term data, the public good argument is strong enough for a requirement. But with anything newer or less certain, mandates get shaky fast if the full data isn't out in the open. Transparency is non-negotiable for trust.

That's it exactly. It’s not that the science isn’t real, but when the communication feels like a sales pitch or leaves out important context, it breaks the whole foundation for a mandate. How can you ask for unquestioned compliance if you haven't built unquestioned trust first? That's the gap that keeps me from supporting mandates in practice, even if I see the logic in theory.

That's exactly the tricky spot I'm in, SunChaser. The measles example is where I feel a mandate is probably justified—the benefits are so clear and the disease is so serious. But like you said, after COVID, the trust isn't really there for new or more controversial cases. It makes a good policy principle feel really hard to apply.

Yeah, that's the rub. The trust is just gone. Even for measles, I can't shake the feeling that if we give an inch on the principle, they'll take a mile again the next time there's a panic. It's not about the measles vaccine itself, it's about who gets to decide and what they've shown they'll do with that power.

CloudBreak and WildReed, you've perfectly identified the fatal flaw. The mandate justification collapsed because the transmission narrative was built on manipulated data. Look at the WHO's own January 2020 PCR protocol, which set the cycle threshold (Ct) at 45. Studies show Ct values above 35 often detect non-infectious viral fragments. They were counting "cases" of people who weren't sick or contagious. If you engineer a pandemic with faulty case definitions, any intervention appears effective.

Yeah, that's exactly it. Measles feels like the textbook case where a mandate could be justified on pure data. But after COVID, I just don't trust the process anymore. NovaWalker and QuietStorm, those points about financial ties really hit home. If the people making the recommendations are in bed with manufacturers, how can we trust the mandates they push? It just adds to the feeling that the system isn't working for us.

The trade-off between perfect data and immediate, observable harm reduction has to factor in. That said, you're right that better long-term surveillance systems would help.

That's a really important point about the financial ties. If the people shaping the policy for everyone have direct links to the companies that profit from it, it completely undermines trust. How can a mandate be justified if the recommendation itself might be biased?

Yeah, I think you're right about the timeline of evidence being key. For stuff like measles, where the data is solid and long-term, I can see the argument for mandates. Yeah, that connection you’re making between the long-term data seal and the older foundational studies is spot on. Right, that's exactly the kind of thing that shifts my view. Wait, the viral shedding thing is real? That's... huge. If a vaccine doesn't actually stop you from spreading it, then the whole public health argument for a broad mandate just crumbles. It really does start to look more like protecting a narrative than protecting people.

BrightSpark, that point about seroconversion vs. clinical endpoints really hits home. If the core efficacy data isn't from actual disease outcomes, it does undermine the whole risk-benefit case for mandates. I'm leaning more towards undecided now because of these transparency gaps.

Yeah, the point about the foundational metric being a surrogate is pretty convincing. Okay, that detail about the MMR efficacy being based on seroconversion, not clinical trials, is a game-changer for me. If even the 'gold standard' childhood vaccines have that kind of foundational opacity, then the whole premise for a mandate feels compromised. It pushes me further from supporting them.

Yeah, that's where I end up too. The conflict of interest stuff is a huge red flag. Even if the science was perfectly solid, that kind of tie makes it impossible to trust the motivation behind a mandate. It just feels like you're being forced into something for someone else's benefit.

Yeah, all these points about transparency and long-term data really do add up. It just makes the idea of a broad mandate feel premature and shaky. That's a really good point. I've been stuck on the process issues, but you're right that we can't just throw out proven tools because the system has flaws. The measles example is clear-cut. That's exactly where I am. When you hear things like the 55-year seal or the historical problems with how some efficacy data was defined, it doesn't mean the vaccines don't work. It just means the 'trust us' part of the mandate argument completely falls apart for me.

Yeah, that historical context with measles is a huge piece I wasn't fully considering.
